408.t: Meeting Charlie Parker and the cherry pie

408.t: Charlie Parker's kindness and playing for Bird at Arthur's

I remember one day he asked me, “did you eat today, young man.” I mean he didn’t know me from a hole in the wall, I was just another alto player licking at his heels, and he said, “did you eat today.” The misconception is that Charlie Parker was stealing everybody’s money and…

Or, he’d be at a bar and there’d be a young guy drinking and uh Gene’d say, “Well, what are you killing yourself over?” [Both laugh] And I remember one time he played with the Johnny Richards band and he just played a blazing solo. 471.t: Beryl Booker, Tootie Heath and the Heath family

471.ch: Bird, Coltrane and Dinah Washington recollections

372.t: Jackie McLean's tribute to Parker's 'Lover Man'
372.s: They discuss McLean reproducing Parker's sick 'Lover Man' solo and Parker's health.

372.t: Strings for Parker and Lester Young

372.q: Well thank you. I always appreciated that situation and wondered why Norman Granz never got that for Lester Young or a real situation . . . for Charlie Parker except that corny string writing that he played so beautifully over.

64.t: Meeting Charlie Parker and talking about reading
64.s: He first met Parker at Birdland when replacing Al Haig, and recalls Parker commenting on his constant reading.
64.ch: New York scene and bebop community
64.q: I guess really the first time I actually met him, I was introduced to him when he was with Earl Hines, but though I had been told about him I didn’t really get to hear him do what Little Benny had said he could so I really wasn’t that interested to be honest with you. I mean my head was somewhere…

64.t: The impact of Charlie Parker's death in 1955
64.s: Parker's death left a sense of urgency; Dizzy became more serious, Clifford Brown rose and attention turned to Monk.
64.q: It wasn’t apparent that his death was going to have the impact that it did. I mean obviously you miss someone who is important to everybody’s developed, who is the major figure, only musician with the nightclub named after him and all that sort of stuff. Charlie Parker, his passing left… gave more…

64.t: Studio work with Bing Crosby; subbing for Al Haig with Parker and strings
64.s: He recounts sneezing during a Bing Crosby take, then being called to replace Al Haig for Charlie Parker with strings at Birdland.
64.q: So I got to record with Bing Crosby and a lot of other people. Bing Crosby… I never will forget that day. It was a very funny day. I had never seen him in person before. I had seen him in the movies and heard him on the radio but here I am you know just a few feet away from this legendary movie and…

409.t: First hearing Parker with Jay McShann
409.s: Cootie first heard Charlie Parker with Jay McShann's band.
409.q: I don't know. But he didn't blend in with my section.

409.s: Parker's friends in the band included Bud Powell and George Treadwell, who met Sarah Vaughan on Amateur Night at the Apollo.
409.q: Well, how he met Sarah Vaughan, my band was playing at the Apollo Theater, and they had Amateur Night, and Sarah Vaughan came on the Amateur Night. And that's how he met Sarah Vaughan.

409.s: Cootie calls Parker the most influential jazz musician; Parker left because Cootie only let him solo, not play parts.
409.q: Trombone, every instrument in the band tried to copy Charlie Parker. And in the history of jazz there has never been one man influence all the instruments.

94.t: Meeting Charlie Parker at a barbecue-place jam session

94.ch: New York, Dallas and Kansas City
94.q: Yeah. I always heard of Charlie Parker. Charlie Parker. Finally, I had my horn Saturday night around one or two o'clock in the morning and we'd be drinking and there was a barbecue place next door, great barbecue, and low and behold a jam session started, cats were blowing, blowing up a storm

94.t: How musicians and audiences took Parker's style
94.s: Moore says musicians understood Parker while listeners did not; he retells how Noble Sissle did not understand Parker's 'Honeysuckle Rose'.
94.ch: New York, Dallas and Kansas City

I would say practically all musicians knew what he was doing but to the other people, the hoi polloi, they don't understand the modern style of what he was doing because it's beyond them, beyond their scope to…

94.t: Charlie Parker afraid to follow Bechet at the Salle Pleyel
94.s: Parker, nervous about following Bechet, was encouraged by Moore; the crowd booed a German band off.

94.q: Kenny Dorham and James Moody and who else was there -- the drummer, Max Roach. Anyway I had finished my set with Hot Lips Page and Don Byas and there's a bar down the basement under the Salle Pleyel where the Festival was and I'm down there and I'm listening to Sidney Bechet hold that audience…

237.t: Lovett on Charlie Parker in Kansas City
237.s: Lovett lived near Parker, says he was too far ahead for local players who would not let him sit in, and walked alone with his horn without a case.
237.ch: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
237.q: I knew him pretty well. He lived a couple of blocks from me on 16th Street, Kansas City, Missouri, and when he first left here and went to New York, he was so far ahead of the alto players playing then that the guys laughed at him for playing so much out that they didn't know anything about and…

237.t: Goodwin on Parker's style and hiring him at Lucille's Paradise
237.s: Goodwin says Parker blended many players' ideas; he hired him at Lucille's Paradise when no one else would.
237.ch: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann

237.ch: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
237.q: Well, I never drank with him. I never had a drink with Charlie. I don't know how he acted after he got a drink in him. I don't know but he was an awful nice guy when I saw him all the time. He wasn't drunk, I'll tell you that much. He wasn't drunk.

239.t: Charlie Parker as a person and dinner at his mother's in Kansas City

23.s: Rose says Parker was skilled but not great, and was influenced by Rudy Vallee and Dick Stabile. He found Parker pleasant, with unfocused protest and little racial self-consciousness.

I believe firmly that the American system has been in decline, demonstrably in decline, since the beginning of World War I. As far as the…

598.t: Declining Max Roach and Bird's wish to hire him

490.s: Parker was kind to the teenage Harris and let him sit in when his band was late.

527.t: Meeting Charlie Parker, staying at their room, the Sentinel review

371.t: Charlie Parker: calm presence, an offer to join his band
371.s: Jones remembers Parker as quiet and businesslike, declined his invitation to join his band, and discusses 'Relaxing at Camarillo'.
371.q: I had the good fortune of playing with Charlie Parker, but never on the road. Except for Jazz at the Philharmonic, I never played within a nightclub setting. But, I was always impressed by his calm approached everything in place. His music was exciting, but he himself was perfectly calm.

564.q: We all – we’d finish our gigs and hurry up and go down to Birdland. That was our hangout after we did our shows around New York and New Jersey and whatever.

375.t: Parker and Tatum, Ray Brown at Minton's, and Dizzy behind the bar
375.s: Shorter thinks Parker listened to Tatum, relays Ray Brown's first sight of Parker, and tells of Dizzy's remark about playing everything he knows in one measure.
375.ch: Teachers, Blakey and Miles on music
375.q: Because it... It doesn’t sound like he was trying to play like a pianist, but there’s something about the essence of the harmonic story, that he could do his own...he was going for or working for his own way of creating that warmth and excitement and adventure and phrases and all that. Because when…

219.t: Playing with Charlie Parker, 'jazz from J to Z' and the first Newport program
219.s: Wein recounts playing Royal Garden Blues with Parker and explains his view of jazz, which shaped the mixed first Newport evening.
219.q: He was a young kid and he was there. Dan is a little younger than I am and I don't know what he was doing, but he remembers that day of Bechet and Tatum. The other thing that we did, we brought up the band from downstairs and Charlie Parker was upstairs and I had Vic Dickenson and Doc Cheatham in…

614.t: Bebop contacts: Dizzy writing, Charlie Parker sitting in, Kansas City tape
614.s: Dizzy Gillespie wrote for the band and Charlie Parker sat in often; an afternoon Kansas City concert was taped and later released by bootleg labels.
614.ch: Decca years and the First Herd
614.q: And then, too, I think the fact that Charlie Parker had made such a big dent into the whole jazz scene, and that we were all very conscious of this, as he, I guess, was conscious of what we were into, because he used to come over and sit in with the band, very often. And that was the reason that…

117.t: Dance challenges Freeman's view of critics
117.s: Dance calls his claim about critics too sweeping and describes growing to hear Charlie Parker; Freeman says the critic idolized only Lester.
117.q: No, no, I am just talking about the misinformed people who have written about jazz and made money. You know what I am talking about, because you and I have been friends for some 30 years.

383.s: Wilson knew Parker only slightly from record dates and a WNEW session; Hinton recalls him as a serious talker who later fell into drugs.
383.q: Not too close. I've made several record dates with him and some jam sessions and jazz concerts. I remember once when I was down at WNEW, he came out a few times as guest with the house band, and they'd have some jazz sessions there.

566.s: Dizzy's friends in the 1940s weren't yet on their own. Humes recorded with Charlie Parker and found him fine, playing blues and everything; after hearing the Basie boys he did not strike her as strange.
566.ch: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
566.q: No, he seemed alright. See I was around them and I knew what most of them did, so I didn't pay them any attention.

148.t: The Ross Russell book and Charlie Parker
148.s: He denies the book's story of an argument with Parker over a Coast date.
148.q: You're repeating something that somebody showed me in a book that was written by Ross Russell, in which Ross Russell was talking about a jazz date that we were doing out on the coast, Bird and Diz and I think Lucky Thompson was on it, Arvin Garrison, myself; it was a bunch of people that Ross…

235.t: Hired for his sound; Bird in Detroit and father on Caruso
235.s: Nicholas says people hired him for his developing sound; he recalls his father hearing Charlie Parker with Andy Kirk and comparing him to Caruso, a standee at the Met.
235.q: I look back on that now...I look back why people hired me is because of my sound. It wasn't really fully developed, but they could see which way I was goin'. They could see and hear that I was tryin' to get a sound.

427.t: Charlie Parker and other Kansas City musicians he met

74.t: Willard Brown, Buster Smith and arrangements
74.s: Brown's drinking and saxophone playing, then Buster Smith's arranging and Charlie Parker's regard for him.
74.ch: Queens Terrace, Decca records and Amen
74.q: Oh, he was a drinker, but he was very peaceful. The only thing he wanted to do was brag about how much he could play, and he could.

236.s: Ben Webster told him about Parker, imitation drove Bird into drugs, and Rowles worked with him.
236.q: Lester had come in there to New York and he scared those guys just like Charlie Parker did! Ben Webster came back down... 86.t: Buster Smith, Charlie Parker's idol, and trips to Kansas City
86.s: Edison says Buster Smith played Parker-like lines before Parker and describes driving from St. Louis to Kansas City.
86.q: Oh, sure it was. He came -- he's the one wrote "One O'Clock Jump," you know. And he was playing like Charlie Parker even before Charlie Parker even thought there was a style he was playing. Bird used to go around and listen to him at the place called the Kansas City Bar-be-que. Used to listen to…

125.t: Buck Clayton in Parsons and Charlie Parker in Kansas City, Kansas
125.s: Jam session with Buck Clayton, home from Count Basie's band, showed Thompson that jazz musicians were gentlemen; he also recalls hearing Charlie Parker in Kansas City.
125.ch: Failure in St. Louis and the Omaha bands
125.q: And that's where I really got introduced to jazz formally by Wilbur, W-i-l-b-u-r, known as Buck, B-u-c-k, last name Clayton, C-l-a-y-t-o-n.

78.t: Phrasing across bar lines before Charlie Parker: Don Redman
78.s: Asked who phrased unusually before Parker, Horace names Don Redman for anticipating bars and out-of-key breaks, before Bird and Dizzy took it further.
78.ch: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
78.q: I know there were a lot of musicians that would anticipate the progression over into the next bar; they would carry them over. And like the first guy, I think, that used to do that was Don Redman, the great alto saxophonist and arranger, in years. In fact, Don used to make a lot of out of key…

455.t: Meeting Charlie Parker at 55th and Michigan in Chicago
455.s: Parker, hoboing into Chicago, blows with Goon Gardner's group and reminds Budd he used to peek into George E. Lee's rehearsals as a Kansas City boy.
455.q: Okay. Well, Charlie Parker -- the first time I met Charlie Parker in person, we were in Chicago. Billy Eckstine had met Charlie Parker before, but I hadn't met Charlie Parker, not, you know -- Charlie Parker knew me, but I didn't know him, and I'll give you a reason why he knew me, because that…

98.t: Keeping the beat at the DeLisa and Regal; Gene Ammons and Charlie Parker sitting in
98.s: His band stayed rhythmic despite younger players; Gene Ammons played with them at the Regal and Parker often came by after working at the Rum Boogie.
98.ch: Regal Theatre, bebop and the Woody Herman date
98.q: Yeah, we had the freedom and things, but we never did relinquish that beat. We didn't get away from that. We always kept that thing going. And we had plenty -- what's her name played with us, not at the Delisa, but at the Regal, Gene Ammons.
